<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A4" title="In Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">D </span>Evaluation Details</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_appendix">

<span id="p1.2.1" class="ltx_ERROR undefined">\model</span>https://huggingface.co/tencent/Youtu-Parsing-Omni</p>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-0.3pt;"><img src="2610.39301v1/figures/penguin.png" id="g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:22/25;" width="22" height="25" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></span> Youtu-Parsing-Omni:
<br class="ltx_break" style="--ltx-break-space:2.0pt;"> One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Youtu-Parsing-Omni Team<sup id="id2" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup>
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We present <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Youtu-Parsing-Omni</span>, an omni-modal parser that converts documents, images, audio, and video into structured records grounded in space and time, providing a perception layer for agents that read, locate, and cite evidence across modalities. Its design rests on one encoder for every modality and one schema for every task. Youtu-Omni-Encoder, initialized from a pre-trained language model to strengthen text reading, encodes all modalities with shared weights in a unified space-time coordinate system, and a few fusion layers let video frames attend to concurrent audio, bringing cross-modal fusion and temporal alignment into perception itself. OmniSchema unifies the outputs of all ten parsing tasks, allowing a single self-evolving post-training procedure, OmniSchema-Aware On-Policy Distillation (OSAD), to provide a shared token-role-based objective across tasks. In each round, the model is trained on its own rollouts against token-level targets from a reference-conditioned copy of itself, which is then refreshed with the trained weights, so that the parser and its supervision co-evolve. With a single <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> B-parameter checkpoint, Youtu-Parsing-Omni achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniDocBench v1.6 (<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="96.96" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>96.96</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">96.96</annotation></semantics></math> Overall) and leads all open-weight models on OmniParsingBench (<math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="75.08" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>75.08</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">75.08</annotation></semantics></math> Avg.), with its advantage concentrated on audio and video. It also achieves the best overall chart-parsing score (<math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95.02" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>95.02</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95.02</annotation></semantics></math>) and the highest exact chemical-fingerprint agreement among compared systems, and matches a dedicated optical-music model in character-level transcription of typeset sheet music while staying far ahead of general-purpose systems. Code and model weights are publicly available.</p>
  
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.39301v1/headline.svg" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/211;" width="476" height="211"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Youtu-Parsing-Omni ranks first on OmniDocBench v1.6 (a), is the strongest open-weight model on OmniParsingBench (b), and also leads on most domain-specific benchmarks (c).</span></figcaption>
</figure><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">*</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">*</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>Author list and contributions are given at the end of the main text.</span></span></span>
<figure id="S0.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.39301v1/overview_figure.png" id="S0.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/314;" width="476" height="314" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S0.F2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="S0.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Omni-modal parsing with one encoder and one schema.</span>
Youtu-Parsing-Omni parses documents, natural images, audio, and video with Youtu-Omni-Encoder shared across all modalities, and unifies their parsing tasks in OmniSchema.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act on information beyond their own parameters: they retrieve evidence before answering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, call tools during reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, and operate computers through the screen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>.
Much of this information arrives not as plain text but as documents, images, audio, and video.
Having the model that drives the agent consume such inputs directly is both <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">costly and hard to audit</em>: each time the agent revisits the material, that model must re-encode long sequences of visual and acoustic tokens, and an answer drawn from raw pixels or waveforms does not by itself indicate which region or interval supports it.
<em id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Omni-modal parsing</em> addresses both issues by converting each input once into a structured text record of <em id="S1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">what</em> it contains and <em id="S1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">where</em> or <em id="S1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">when</em> each part occurs.
Any LLM, including a text-only one, can then read and act on this record and trace a claim back to its source through the anchors it cites; parsing thus provides a perception layer between non-text inputs and language-model reasoning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Current parsers, however, cover this range of inputs only partially.
Document parsers have become strong on standard pages <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, but symbolic content such as chemical structures and sheet music is still left largely to domain-specific models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.
Beyond documents, parsing is even less mature.
Omni-modal models are built mainly for captioning and question answering rather than for grounded, structured output <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, and parsing across images, audio, and video has only recently been formulated as a task with a dedicated benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>.
As a result, different input types are typically served by different models with different output formats.
Yet the target output is the same across input types, namely a structured record whose units are anchored in space or time, which suggests building a single parser with one output schema rather than one specialist per input type.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Building such a parser raises two challenges.
<span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(C1) Joint perception across modalities.</span>
Omni-modal models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> and the omni-modal parser Logics-Parsing-Omni <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> pair two separately pre-trained encoders, one for vision and one for audio, an arrangement with three consequences.
First, each modality is encoded in isolation: no cross-modal fusion takes place during perception, and the language model must infer cross-modal relations from separate representations.
Second, the two encoders index time independently, so a frame and the sound of the same instant do not share temporal positions within perception; temporal alignment, where modeled, is deferred to the language model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>.
Third, each encoder requires its own architecture, training objective, and pre-training, so perception parameters are not shared across modalities and each new modality requires another tower.
The first two consequences weigh more on parsing than on captioning or question answering, because a structured parse must state explicitly which content co-occurs across modalities and when.
Encoders shared across vision and audio have been explored <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, but, to our knowledge, not for grounded parsing.
<span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(C2) Joint optimization across tasks.</span>
The same model must also be optimized jointly for content accuracy, spatial and temporal grounding, and schema validity across ten tasks whose output fields differ.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains only on reference prefixes, never on the prefixes the model itself produces at inference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>.
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), including Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, is increasingly used in document parsing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>; it trains on the model’s own outputs but requires a scalar reward that is hard to define across such heterogeneous criteria and provides only sequence-level feedback.
On-policy distillation supplies token-level targets on the model’s own outputs using accessible teacher distributions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. Reference-conditioned self-distillation can instead obtain these targets from the same model under an enriched context <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>; the remaining question is how to adapt this supervision to heterogeneous schema roles and refresh it as the parser learns.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To address both challenges, we present Youtu-Parsing-Omni, <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">an omni-modal parser built on one encoder for every modality and one schema for every task</em> (Fig. <a href="#S0.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
For C1, <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">a unified perception encoder</span>, Youtu-Omni-Encoder, replaces the two towers with one shared Transformer initialized from a pre-trained text language model to strengthen text reading.
Only lightweight input stems and output projectors remain modality-specific, so almost all perception parameters are shared across modalities.
Visual and acoustic tokens share one space-time positional encoding and interact in a few fusion layers, so a frame and the sound of the same instant are aligned and fused within short audio-visual windows inside perception, leaving only dependencies across windows to the language model.
For C2, the shared schema allows <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">a single self-evolving post-training procedure</span>, OmniSchema-Aware On-Policy Distillation (OSAD), to use the same token-role-based objective across tasks after SFT and schema-routed RLVR.
Instead of a sequence-level reward, the model learns from token-level targets on its own parses, provided by a frozen copy of itself that additionally conditions on the reference parse <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>.
Because every output follows OmniSchema, each token can be identified as content or structure and supervised with an objective suited to its role.
After each round, the trained student becomes the next teacher, so the supervision evolves with the parser; OSAD itself thus requires neither a hand-designed reward nor a separately trained teacher.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">With this design, a single <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> B-parameter Youtu-Parsing-Omni checkpoint serves all ten parsing tasks and achieves <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">state-of-the-art document parsing</em>, scoring <math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="96.96" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>96.96</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">96.96</annotation></semantics></math> on OmniDocBench v1.6 (Fig. <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>a).
On OmniParsingBench, it leads open-weight models with a score of <math id="S1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="75.08" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>75.08</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">75.08</annotation></semantics></math>, surpassing Logics-Parsing-Omni (<math id="S1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="72.26" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>72.26</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">72.26</annotation></semantics></math>), with its largest gains on audio and video (Fig. <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>b).
The same checkpoint also excels at <em id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">symbolic transcription</em> (Fig. <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>c).
On chemical structures, it reaches an exact fingerprint-match rate (Tani@1.0) of <math id="S1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="54.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>54.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">54.2</annotation></semantics></math>, outperforming DeepSeek-OCR 2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> (<math id="S1.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="49.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>49.6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">49.6</annotation></semantics></math>).
On typeset sheet music, it achieves a character error rate (CER) of <math id="S1.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="22.73" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>22.73</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">22.73</annotation></semantics></math>, on par with the specialist LEGATO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> (<math id="S1.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="23.30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>23.30</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">23.30</annotation></semantics></math>, as reported in its original paper). Together, these results show that <em id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">one encoder and one schema can support broad multimodal parsing while retaining the precision of specialized models</em>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.39301v1/arch_figure.png" id="S1.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/244;" width="476" height="244" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S1.F3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="S1.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Overview of omni-modal parsing architectures.</span>
We compare how visual and audio inputs are encoded before reaching the language model in the conventional design and in Youtu-Parsing-Omni.
(a) Existing omni-modal parsers encode pixels and audio with two separately pre-trained towers, whose streams first meet inside the language model.
(b) Youtu-Parsing-Omni replaces both towers with a single encoder, Youtu-Omni-Encoder. Thin modality-specific stems map pixels and log-mel frames to tokens; a shared bidirectional block then contextualizes an arbitrary packed mix of images, audio chunks, and videos under one <math id="S1.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(t,h,w)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(t,h,w)</annotation></semantics></math> positional encoding; and a few of its layers (red) attend across modalities within short audio-visual windows (Fig. <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Stems. ‣ 2.1 Youtu-Omni-Encoder ‣ 2 Model ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).
As a result, pixels and sound share weights and positional encoding, and interact already inside the encoder.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Model</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Youtu-Parsing-Omni is a decoder-only language model fed by one perception encoder (Fig. <a href="#S1.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
It accepts text, images, audio, and video (with its audio track when present) and emits text only.
The decoder is a dense text language model pre-trained following the recipe of Youtu-LLM-2B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>; it keeps 1D rotary positions, since spatial and temporal structure is already resolved inside the encoder (App. <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Language Model ‣ Appendix B Architecture Details ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>).
Further architectural details, including the variants that the final model does not use, are given in App. <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Architecture Details ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>, and the complete configuration in Tab. <a href="#A2.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ B.1 Model Specification ‣ Appendix B Architecture Details ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>.
Two principles shape the encoder.
First, every modality is read by the same weights with the same space-time positional encoding (Subsec. <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Youtu-Omni-Encoder ‣ 2 Model ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>–<a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Unified Positional Encoding and Audio-Visual Fusion ‣ 2 Model ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>).
Second, these weights start from a model that already maps context to symbols (Subsec. <a href="#S5.SS7.SSS0.Px2" title="Effect of text-LM initialization. ‣ 5.7 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Evaluation ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.7</span></a>).
The first principle thus amortizes perception capacity across modalities rather than duplicating it in one tower per modality.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Youtu-Omni-Encoder</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Vision and audio inputs pass through a three-part pipeline whose middle part is shared: a modality-specific stem turns raw input into <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional tokens, a shared Transformer contextualizes them, and a modality-specific merger and projector down-sample the result and map it to the decoder width.
Only the stems and the merger–projector heads depend on the modality; together they hold a small fraction of the encoder’s parameters (App. <a href="#A2.SS2.SSS1" title="B.2.1 Modality Stems ‣ B.2 Youtu-Omni-Encoder ‣ Appendix B Architecture Details ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2.1</span></a>), so most of the encoder is shared.
Architecturally, adding a modality therefore requires a new stem and projector rather than a second tower with its own pre-training lineage, although the shared weights must still be trained on the new input.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Stems.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The two stems convert raw signals into tokens with minimal machinery.
Images and video frames are cut into fixed-size patches at their native resolution under a token budget <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, and a single linear map turns each patch into one token; no further convolution, absolute position table, or class token is used.
Audio is converted to a log-mel spectrogram, and a few strided convolutions down-sample it in time before a linear map to width <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>, giving a fixed audio token rate of <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> tokens per second.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.39301v1/mech_figure.svg" id="S2.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/155;" width="476" height="155"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S2.F4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="S2.F4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Concurrent visual and audio content share fusion windows and a common temporal coordinate system.</span>
(a) A video with eight frames (I) and four audio chunks (A), packed in temporal order, with each chunk placed after the frames it overlaps.
A non-fusion layer gives every frame and every chunk its own window;
a fusion layer starts a new window at every audio-to-frame boundary, so the video forms four <math id="S2.F4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathrm{I}^{+}\mathrm{A}^{*})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathrm{I}^{+}\mathrm{A}^{*})</annotation></semantics></math> windows; red cells mark the cross-modal pairs, and off-diagonal blue cells the frame-to-frame pairs, that only fusion layers admit.
(b) Vision tokens take <math id="S2.F4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> from the frame index and <math id="S2.F4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(h,w)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(h,w)</annotation></semantics></math> from the patch grid; audio tokens take <math id="S2.F4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> from their offset and write into the same temporal rotary slots.
Inside a fusion window both advance on the common time scale of Equ. <a href="#S2.E1" title="In Windows and time alignment. ‣ 2.2 Unified Positional Encoding and Audio-Visual Fusion ‣ 2 Model ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Shared Transformer blocks.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The shared Transformer is a stack of standard pre-norm blocks with RMSNorm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, SwiGLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, grouped-query attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>, and QK-Norm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>.
Attention is bidirectional.
Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> are applied from a matrix of per-token rotation angles rather than read from one position table shared by the whole sequence; this is what makes the axis-factorized positional encoding of Subsec. <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Unified Positional Encoding and Audio-Visual Fusion ‣ 2 Model ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a> expressible.
Any mix of images, audio chunks, and videos is packed into one variable-length sequence whose attention windows are given by a cumulative-length vector <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>, so one encoder pass handles the whole mix without padding.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Token merger and projector.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After the shared Transformer, neighboring vision tokens within a frame are concatenated along the feature axis into one token, and adjacent audio tokens are merged in the same way along time.
Each modality then passes through an RMSNorm and a two-layer MLP that projects it to the decoder width.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Unified Positional Encoding and Audio-Visual Fusion</h3>

<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">One positional encoding for all modalities.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Sharing one Transformer across modalities makes positional encoding the central design question: one rotary budget of frequency slots has to express 2D layout, 1D time, and the correspondence between the two.
We partition the budget into contiguous segments of near-equal size, one for each axis <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math>, each with its own inverse-frequency table normalized by its own width, so every axis spans the full frequency range regardless of how many slots it receives (Equ. <a href="#A2.E7" title="In Chunked axis-factorized RoPE. ‣ B.2.3 Positional Encoding ‣ B.2 Youtu-Omni-Encoder ‣ Appendix B Architecture Details ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, App. <a href="#A2.SS2.SSS3" title="B.2.3 Positional Encoding ‣ B.2 Youtu-Omni-Encoder ‣ Appendix B Architecture Details ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2.3</span></a>).
A vision token takes <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> from its frame index and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(h,w)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(h,w)</annotation></semantics></math> from its patch position; an audio token takes <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> from its time offset and sets <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=w=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=w=0</annotation></semantics></math>.
Both modalities therefore write into the same <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> segment, expressing their temporal positions on a common time scale.
Modality identity is left to the features: the two stems produce readily separable feature distributions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The shared timeline makes frame and audio positions comparable, but it does not by itself let them interact.
Fusion provides this interaction by letting the two attend to each other, so that the correspondence a video parse must output (for instance, which words are spoken while a given slide is on screen) is computed in perception rather than reconstructed by the decoder.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Fused and independent routes.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A video reaches the encoder by either of two routes that share all weights and return outputs of identical shape.
On the <em id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">independent</em> route, each frame and each audio chunk forms its own attention window, as if the input were a burst of images and an unrelated recording.
On the <em id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">fused</em> route, the frames and audio chunks of one video are packed in temporal order, and in the fusion layers audio-visual windows let a frame attend to the sound of the same instant; the other layers keep one window per frame or chunk.
During training, a video takes the fused route with probability <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathrm{fus}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>fus</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathrm{fus}}</annotation></semantics></math>, set below <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> from Stage 2 on (Sec. <a href="#S4" title="4 Training ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>), which keeps both routes usable at inference.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Windows and time alignment.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On the fused route, the packed event list (e.g., <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\mathrm{I}_{1},\mathrm{I}_{2},\mathrm{A}_{1},\mathrm{I}_{3},\dots]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\mathrm{I}_{1},\mathrm{I}_{2},\mathrm{A}_{1},\mathrm{I}_{3},\dots]</annotation></semantics></math>) is cut into <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathrm{I}^{+}\mathrm{A}^{*})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathrm{I}^{+}\mathrm{A}^{*})</annotation></semantics></math> groups, i.e., one or more frames followed by the audio chunks that precede the next frame, with a new group starting at every audio-to-frame boundary; in the fusion layers, each group becomes one attention window (Fig. <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Stems. ‣ 2.1 Youtu-Omni-Encoder ‣ 2 Model ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>a).
Inside a group, vision and audio advance on a common time scale tied to the audio token rate,</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta t_{\text{audio}}=1\ \text{per token},\qquad\Delta t_{\text{vision}}=\frac{r_{a}}{\mathrm{fps}}\ \text{per frame}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mtext>audio</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>per token</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mtext>vision</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mi>fps</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>per frame</mtext></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta t_{\text{audio}}=1\ \text{per token},\qquad\Delta t_{\text{vision}}=\frac{r_{a}}{\mathrm{fps}}\ \text{per frame},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{fps}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>fps</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{fps}</annotation></semantics></math> is the sampled video frame rate and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> is the audio token rate of the audio stem, before merging. This places frames and audio tokens on a common time scale, without requiring every sampled frame to coincide with a discrete audio-token position (Fig. <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Stems. ‣ 2.1 Youtu-Omni-Encoder ‣ 2 Model ‣ Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>b).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Sparse fusion.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Because windows are specified only by <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}</annotation></semantics></math>, fusion is a per-layer choice: the same packed features carry a per-group segmentation <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}^{\text{fus}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐜</mi><mtext>fus</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}^{\text{fus}}</annotation></semantics></math> and a per-event (non-fusion) segmentation <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}^{\text{nof}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐜</mi><mtext>nof</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}^{\text{nof}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and each layer uses one of them.
The two segmentations assign different time origins to the same token, which is harmless because a rotary attention score depends only on the offset <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{q}-t_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{q}-t_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> between query and key positions, and queries never meet keys from another window.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

id="lstnumberx49.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">":</span><span id="lstnumberx49.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx49.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">"</span><span id="lstnumberx49.7" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">zh</span><span id="lstnumberx49.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx49.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">|</span><span id="lstnumberx49.10" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx49.11" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">en</span><span id="lstnumberx49.12" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx49.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">|</span><span id="lstnumberx49.14" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">"</span><span id="lstnumberx49.17" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">                           </span><span id="lstnumberx49.18" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">//</span><span id="lstnumberx49.19" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx49.20" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">audio</span><span id="lstnumberx49.21" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter"
